newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Collins film set to break Irish box office records.
newsitem.headline: Collins film set to break Irish box office records.

text.p: A controversial film about Michael Collins, a leading figure in the creation of modern Ireland, has its premiere on Wednesday and is poised to break all records when it goes on general release.
"I've never seen anything like this before. It should beat all box office records," Ita Bourke of Ward Anderson, which runs a number of Irish cinemas, said.

The $28 million Hollywood drama "Michael Collins" will open in 120 cinemas across Ireland on Thursday following premieres in both Dublin and Cork, and has attracted a record number of advance bookings.

The film features "Schindler's List" star Liam Neeson as Collins, the man who masterminded Ireland's fight for independence from British rule but was shot in the ensuing civil war after he signed an Anglo-Irish Treaty in December 1921.
But Jordan's drama, which won the best film and best actor awards and a 10-minute standing ovation at the Venice film festival, has provoked praise and criticism in almost equal measure.
Jordan has been accused of historical inaccuracy and of inflaming passions at a sensitive time in the Northern Ireland peace process.
Arriving at a windswept Cork airport on Tuesday, Jordan said he wished that people had first seen the film before passing judgement.
"It's a tough job getting all that history down into a two-hour movie. I did my best and it is accurate in the broad spirit of the history of the time."
The film, which also features Julia Roberts, has divided opionion in Northern Ireland, where its release comes at a particularly troubled time in the search for a permanent peace.

Irish Republican Army guerrillas, who trace their origins to the army Collins led to fight British rule, bombed Britain's Northern Ireland army base near Belfast last month, bringing war back to the province after a two-year respite.

"If the film makes a contribution towards a greater understanding of the history of the island, and the total futility of violence, it will have been an extremely worthwhile exercise," the Belfast newspaper, The Irish News, said in an editorial on Wednesday.
But others are concerned that it could lead impressionable young Catholics to back the underground IRA, which is illegal in the province and in Ireland.
